questions.q: What is the main advantage of the logging module over using print() for diagnostic output?
options: logging is faster to type than print()
logging supports severity levels, timestamps, and multiple destinations like a file or console
print() cannot output text to the terminal at all
logging automatically fixes bugs in the script
questions.explain: logging adds severity levels (DEBUG through CRITICAL), timestamps, and the ability to route messages to multiple handlers (file, console, etc.) — none of which plain print() provides.

questions.q: Which of these lists the logging levels from least to most severe?
options: CRITICAL, ERROR, WARNING, INFO, DEBUG
DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL
INFO, DEBUG, ERROR, WARNING, CRITICAL
WARNING, ERROR, DEBUG, INFO, CRITICAL
questions.explain: The standard order is DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL, from least to most severe.

questions.q: In a try/except block handling several server connections, why catch a specific exception like ConnectionError before a broad `except Exception`?
options: Python requires exceptions to be listed alphabetically
It lets you react differently to an expected failure versus any other unexpected error
Specific exceptions run faster than generic ones
It prevents the except block from ever running
questions.explain: Catching a specific exception type first lets you handle an expected failure mode distinctly, while a broader except Exception still catches anything else unanticipated.

questions.q: What is a custom exception, such as `class HealthCheckError(Exception): pass`?
options: A built-in Python exception that must be imported
A class that inherits from Exception to name a specific failure condition in your own code
A function that logs errors to a file
A way to disable exception handling entirely
questions.explain: A custom exception is a class inheriting from Exception (or a subclass of it), used to represent a specific, named failure condition rather than relying only on generic exceptions.

questions.q: In a simple retry loop that tries a connection up to max_attempts times, when should the final custom exception be raised?
options: Before any attempt is made
After every attempt has failed, once the retry loop is exhausted
Only if the first attempt fails
Retry logic should never raise an exception
questions.explain: A retry loop should keep trying up to the attempt limit, logging each failure, and only raise the final exception once all attempts have been exhausted without success.
